The security review is complete. The report validates as proper JSON, the only new file is `SECURITY_REVIEW.json`, and no audited source files were modified.

## Summary

I reviewed all 10 source/config files in the repository (no `package.json`/lockfile/deps exist, so no dependency audit was applicable). I traced untrusted inputs to dangerous sinks and avoided pattern-only false positives (e.g., the path-traversal guard in `src/routes/avatar.js` is actually correct with its `ROOT + path.sep` check, and that router isn't even mounted, so it was not flagged).

**Two exploitable findings:**

1. **`broken-object-level-authorization` (HIGH)** — `GET /api/invoices/:id` authenticates the caller and extracts a `tenantId` from the JWT, but the invoice lookup (`findById`) queries `where id = $1` with no tenant filter. Despite the repo exposing a tenant-scoped `listForTenant`, the per-object path skips tenant isolation, letting any authenticated user read any other tenant's invoice by id.

2. **`mass-assignment` (HIGH)** — `PATCH /api/profile` passes `req.body` straight through `users.update(...)` into `db.users.update({ id }, fields)` with no field allowlist. Only the lookup id comes from the trusted JWT; the attacker controls every column, enabling self-promotion to `role: admin`, tenant pivoting (`tenant_id`), or id rewriting.

The taxonomy categories I explicitly considered and ruled out as non-exploitable here: SQL injection (all queries use `$1` parameterization), authentication bypass (JWT verified with pinned `HS256` + env secret, no `alg:none` confusion), hardcoded secret (secret is `process.env`), path traversal (avatar guard is correct and route unmounted), and vulnerable dependency (no dependency metadata present).
